newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU clears ship aid in Germany, Greece, Spain.
newsitem.headline: EU clears ship aid in Germany, Greece, Spain.

text.p: EU industry ministers gave the green light on Thursday to state aid totalling some $1.6 billion to ailing German, Spanish and Greek shipyards despite strong opposition from the bloc's three Nordic member states.

The European Commission's proposal to approve the requests of Bonn, Athens and Madrid for permission to grant the restructuring support, which has sparked U.S. criticism, won the necessary backing of a qualified majority of EU countries.

The ministers, increasingly pessmistic about the chances of U.S. ratification of a plan to slash shipbuilding subsidies, also agreed to extend existing EU ship aid rules for another year until the end of 1998.
Finland and Sweden, preferring to see stricter aid rules as soon as possible, also voted against this decision.

However, the bloc's aid rules -- which allow for up to nine percent of contract-related aid -- lapses automatically if Washington succeeds in winning approval in the Republican-controlled Congress for the deal struck within the OECD.
In addition, the European Commission plans to present proposals for a new EU aid regime before the end of the summer which could replace present rules.

Most member states said they were in favour of new legislation on support to the sector in the absence of U.S. ratification of the deal within the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.
EU Competition Commissioner Karel van Miert told a press conference his proposal would introduce the "one time, last time" principle for restructuring aid to shipyards.
The EU executive had delayed a decision on the ship aid in Germany, Spain and Greece, waiting for U.S. ratification of the OECD deal.
But it decided to go ahead with its proposal to EU industry ministers after a meeting last month of the OECD, the club of wealthy industrial nations, failed to produce an outcome.
However, Van Miert tried to ease concerns among other shipbuilders, saying the aid would not significantly boost the yards' competitive position.
Germany, Spain and Greece had undertaken not to pay any more rescue or restructuring aid to the shipyards. "All governments say this is the last time they ask for aid," he told reporters.
The EU executive also insisted on important reductions in production capacity in Germany and Spain and there would be strict monitoring of the conditions imposed on the shipyards.
The German aid would help two shipyards in former east Germany previously owned by bankrupt Bremer Vulkan.
The problems of MTW-Schiffswerft and Volkswerft Stralsund arose from alleged misuse by Bremer Vulkan of 850 million marks ($495 million) in subsidies intended for them.
Of the needed aid of around one billion marks, 728 million marks would require the approval of EU industry ministers.
In Greece, the proposal would allow Athens to write off 54.5 billion drachmas ($201 million) in debts accumulated by Hellenic shipyards before it was privatised in 1995.

The Spanish support was needed for restructuring public yards to return them to viability by the end of 1998. It concerned aid of some 135 billion pesetas in interest payments, tax credits and capital injection.

EU officials insist the proposed aid would have been allowed also if the OECD deal had been in force as the restructuring cases were agreed before it had been signed. That accord is designed to end direct shipbuilding subsidies except social aid, and research and development aid.
However, U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky last month expressed "dismay" at the proposal by the EU executive to clear the aid in the three countries.
($1 = 270 drachmas)
($1 = 143.9 pesetas)
